mcqs.question: Why is cache invalidation considered one of the genuinely hard problems in computer science?
options: Because storing a copy of data in a cache is technically difficult
Because knowing the exact moment a cached copy stops matching reality, across every place it's been copied, is hard to coordinate correctly
Because most caching libraries don't support deleting entries
Because it only matters for very large-scale systems
mcqs.explanation: The difficulty isn't storing the copy — it's reliably knowing and propagating the moment that copy becomes wrong, across every layer it might live in. Storing data is easy and well-supported by every caching library; this problem shows up at any scale, including a single app server with one cache.

mcqs.question: What's the key trade-off between TTL expiry and explicit invalidation?
options: TTL expiry requires no coordination but guarantees a staleness window; explicit invalidation has no staleness window but requires every write path to remember to trigger it
TTL expiry is always faster to implement and always more correct
Explicit invalidation eliminates the need for a cache entirely
TTL expiry only works for read-through caches, never for cache-aside
mcqs.explanation: TTL trades coordination-free simplicity for a guaranteed (if bounded) staleness window; explicit invalidation removes that window but pushes the burden onto every writer to trigger it correctly. TTL isn't universally "more correct," explicit invalidation doesn't remove the cache, and TTL works with any caching pattern, not just read-through.

mcqs.question: A cache cluster broadcasts invalidations asynchronously across its nodes. What can happen as a result?
options: Nothing — asynchronous invalidation is always instant in practice
The cluster automatically pauses all reads until every node confirms invalidation
Two users hitting different nodes at the same moment can legitimately see different answers for the same key
Every node in the cluster must have identical data at all times by design
mcqs.explanation: Async fan-out means some nodes invalidate before others, so a real window exists where different nodes disagree on the same key — that's the whole risk of the pattern. It isn't instant, clusters don't pause reads to wait for full propagation by default, and "always identical" is precisely the guarantee async invalidation lacks.

mcqs.question: How do versioned cache keys (e.g. app.a1b2c3.js) avoid invalidation races entirely?
options: Old and new versions of the data live under different keys, so there's never a moment where the current key serves a stale value
They compress the cached data so it takes up less memory
They automatically detect and delete the old version the instant the new one is written
They replace the need for TTLs across the whole system
mcqs.explanation: Because the new content gets a new key, the old key's value is never overwritten or contested — it just ages out naturally while the current key always points at the current version. This has nothing to do with compression, doesn't require any automatic deletion step, and TTLs are still useful elsewhere in the system.

mcqs.question: Why is invalidating the cache before the database write commits a risky ordering?
options: A concurrent reader can miss the now-empty cache, read the still-old value from the database, and re-populate the cache with that stale value
It's not risky — invalidating early is always the safer choice
It causes the database write itself to fail
It only matters for write-behind caches, not cache-aside
mcqs.explanation: Invalidating first opens a window where a concurrent read misses, falls through to the database (which hasn't committed the new value yet), and writes the stale result right back into the cache — where it can sit until TTL expiry. This ordering is a genuine risk, doesn't touch whether the DB write itself succeeds, and the race applies broadly, not only to write-behind.
